title: Limnology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Plant/Aquatic Science limnology curriculum: scope of limnology, lake origin and morphometry, physical stratification (light, thermal layering, mixing regimes), chemical properties (oxygen, nutrients, eutrophication), lake and river zonation, plankton and benthos, primary productivity, trophic classification, aquatic macrophytes, and water pollution/quality assessment.

questions.question: Limnology is best defined as the scientific study of:
options: Inland (freshwater) waters, including lakes, rivers, ponds and wetlands
questions.correct_answer: Inland (freshwater) waters, including lakes, rivers, ponds and wetlands
questions.explanation: Limnology (from Greek 'limne', lake/pool) is the interdisciplinary study of the biological, chemical and physical features of inland waters -- lakes, ponds, rivers, streams and wetlands.

questions.question: A body of standing (non-flowing) water such as a lake or pond is described as a:
questions.explanation: Lentic refers to still or standing water bodies (lakes, ponds, reservoirs), in contrast to lotic systems, which are flowing waters such as rivers and streams.

questions.question: Rivers and streams, characterised by continuously flowing water, are classified as:
questions.explanation: Lotic ecosystems are defined by unidirectional, flowing water, which shapes their physical structure and the adaptations of their organisms differently from still lentic waters.

questions.question: Lakes formed by the damming of a river valley behind glacial moraine, landslide debris, or a constructed dam are classified by origin as:
questions.explanation: Barrier or dam lakes form when a natural obstruction (moraine, landslide, lava flow) or an artificial dam blocks a river valley, impounding water; Kainji Lake in Nigeria is a man-made example.

questions.question: Lakes occupying depressions formed by movements of the earth's crust (faulting/downwarping), such as the African Rift Valley lakes, are called:
questions.explanation: Tectonic lakes occupy basins created by crustal movements such as faulting; the deep Rift Valley lakes of East Africa (e.g. Lake Tanganyika) are classic examples.

questions.question: A crescent-shaped lake formed when a meandering river cuts off one of its bends is called an:
questions.explanation: Oxbow lakes form on floodplains when a river meander is isolated from the main channel as the river cuts a new, straighter course, leaving a crescent-shaped standing water body.

questions.question: The study of the physical dimensions of a lake basin -- area, depth, volume and shoreline shape -- is called:
questions.explanation: Lake morphometry describes quantitative aspects of basin shape (surface area, maximum and mean depth, volume, shoreline development index), which strongly influence a lake's physical and biological processes.

questions.question: In lake morphometry, the shoreline development index measures:
options: The irregularity of the shoreline relative to a circle of equal area
The maximum depth of the lake
questions.correct_answer: The irregularity of the shoreline relative to a circle of equal area
questions.explanation: The shoreline development index compares the actual shoreline length to the circumference of a perfect circle enclosing the same lake area; higher values indicate a more irregular, indented shoreline, which affects littoral habitat extent.

questions.question: As sunlight penetrates a water body, the depth beyond which photosynthesis can no longer exceed respiration is the lower boundary of the:
questions.explanation: The euphotic zone extends from the surface down to the depth where light intensity permits net positive photosynthesis (commonly taken as ~1% of surface light); below it lies the aphotic zone where respiration exceeds photosynthesis.

questions.question: In a thermally stratified temperate lake in summer, the warm, less dense surface layer is called the:
questions.explanation: The epilimnion is the uppermost, warmest, well-mixed layer of a stratified lake, overlying the metalimnion (thermocline) and the colder, denser hypolimnion below.

questions.question: The zone of rapid temperature change (steep thermal gradient) separating the epilimnion from the hypolimnion is called the:
questions.explanation: The thermocline, within the metalimnion, is the layer where temperature drops most sharply with depth, acting as a physical barrier that limits mixing between the epilimnion and hypolimnion during stratification.

questions.question: The cold, dense bottom layer of a stratified lake, often poor in dissolved oxygen by late summer, is called the:
questions.explanation: The hypolimnion is the deep, cold, denser bottom layer that is isolated from atmospheric reoxygenation during stratification, so its oxygen can become depleted by decomposition of settling organic matter.

questions.question: A dimictic lake is one that:
options: Mixes completely twice a year, in spring and autumn, due to seasonal turnover
Never mixes at any time of year
Freezes completely to the bottom every winter
questions.correct_answer: Mixes completely twice a year, in spring and autumn, due to seasonal turnover
questions.explanation: Dimictic lakes, typical of temperate regions, undergo two complete vertical mixing (turnover) events per year -- spring and fall overturn -- as temperature (and hence density) differences between surface and bottom water temporarily disappear.

questions.question: Most shallow tropical lakes, including many in Nigeria, are best described as:
options: Polymictic (mixing frequently, even daily, due to small day-night temperature differences)
Meromictic (never mixing due to permanent chemical stratification) in all cases
questions.correct_answer: Polymictic (mixing frequently, even daily, due to small day-night temperature differences)
questions.explanation: Shallow tropical lakes generally experience small diel temperature ranges and only weak, easily disrupted stratification, so they tend to mix frequently (polymictic), unlike temperate dimictic lakes with strong seasonal thermal differences.

questions.question: Density of fresh water is at its maximum at approximately:
questions.explanation: Pure fresh water has its maximum density at about 4 degrees Celsius; water is less dense both above and below this temperature, which is why ice floats and why dimictic lakes stratify and overturn as described.

questions.question: Dissolved oxygen concentration in a stratified eutrophic lake typically shows which profile in the hypolimnion during summer stagnation?
options: Progressive depletion (clinograde curve) due to decomposition of organic matter with no reoxygenation
No change from the surface value
questions.correct_answer: Progressive depletion (clinograde curve) due to decomposition of organic matter with no reoxygenation
questions.explanation: In productive (eutrophic) stratified lakes, decomposer respiration in the isolated hypolimnion consumes oxygen faster than it can be replenished, producing a clinograde oxygen curve with severe depletion near the bottom.

questions.question: The process by which excessive nutrient enrichment (especially nitrogen and phosphorus) leads to algal blooms and subsequent oxygen depletion in a water body is called:
questions.explanation: Eutrophication is nutrient over-enrichment (often from agricultural runoff or sewage) that stimulates excessive algal/plant growth; the subsequent decomposition of this biomass depletes dissolved oxygen, harming aquatic life.

questions.question: In most freshwater systems, the nutrient most commonly identified as the limiting factor for algal growth (and hence the main target of eutrophication control) is:
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is frequently the limiting nutrient in freshwater lakes (nitrogen is more often limiting in marine systems), so phosphorus inputs from detergents, fertilisers and sewage are a principal driver of freshwater eutrophication.

questions.question: A lake with low nutrient concentrations, high water clarity, and low biological productivity is classified as:
questions.explanation: Oligotrophic lakes have low nutrient loading, clear water, high dissolved oxygen throughout the water column, and relatively low primary productivity, in contrast to nutrient-rich, highly productive eutrophic lakes.

questions.question: A dystrophic lake is characterised by:
options: High humic (dissolved organic) matter content, brownish water colour, and low pH
Crystal-clear water with very low organic content
Complete absence of any organic matter
questions.correct_answer: High humic (dissolved organic) matter content, brownish water colour, and low pH
questions.explanation: Dystrophic lakes, often associated with bog/peat-influenced catchments, are stained brown by humic acids, tend to be acidic, and have low productivity despite high organic carbon content.

questions.question: The nearshore zone of a lake where light penetrates to the bottom and rooted aquatic macrophytes can grow is the:
questions.explanation: The littoral zone is the shallow, well-lit margin of a lake where sufficient light reaches the bottom to support rooted and attached macrophytes and associated fauna.

questions.question: The open-water zone of a lake beyond the littoral, extending down to the limit of effective light penetration and dominated by plankton, is the:
questions.explanation: The limnetic or pelagic zone is the open-water region beyond the littoral, within the euphotic zone, dominated by phytoplankton, zooplankton and fish rather than rooted vegetation.

questions.question: The deep, dimly lit or dark bottom zone of a lake, below the limit of effective photosynthesis, is called the:
questions.explanation: The profundal zone lies below the euphotic zone in deep lakes, receiving little or no light, and is characterised by organisms adapted to darkness and often low oxygen, relying on organic matter sinking from above.

questions.question: Free-floating microscopic algae that form the base of most aquatic food webs are known as:
questions.explanation: Phytoplankton are photosynthetic, mostly microscopic organisms (diatoms, green algae, cyanobacteria, etc.) suspended in the water column that are the principal primary producers of open-water ecosystems.

questions.question: Small floating/drifting animals such as rotifers, copepods and cladocerans (e.g. Daphnia) that graze on phytoplankton are collectively called:
questions.explanation: Zooplankton are heterotrophic planktonic animals that graze on phytoplankton and bacteria, forming a key link transferring energy to higher trophic levels such as planktivorous fish.

questions.question: Organisms that live in or on the bottom sediments of a water body (e.g. bottom-dwelling insect larvae, molluscs, worms) are collectively known as:
questions.explanation: Benthos refers to organisms associated with the lake or river bottom (sediment surface or substrate), distinct from plankton (drifting) and nekton (actively swimming organisms like fish).

questions.question: Rooted or attached aquatic plants visible to the naked eye, including submerged, floating-leaved and emergent forms, are collectively termed:
questions.explanation: Aquatic macrophytes are macroscopic plants of aquatic habitats, including submerged forms (e.g. Ceratophyllum), floating forms (e.g. water hyacinth) and emergent forms (e.g. Typha), important as habitat and primary producers, especially in the littoral zone.

questions.question: Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), a notorious invasive aquatic weed in many Nigerian water bodies, is classified structurally as a:
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth floats freely on the water surface with its roots dangling unattached in the water column, distinguishing it from rooted submerged or emergent macrophytes; it can form dense mats that block light, navigation and oxygen exchange.

questions.question: Attached algae and associated microorganisms that grow on submerged surfaces such as rocks, macrophytes or artificial substrates are called:
questions.explanation: Periphyton (also called aufwuchs) is the community of algae, bacteria and microfauna attached to submerged surfaces, contributing significantly to primary production, especially in shallow and lotic systems.

questions.question: In river ecology, the River Continuum Concept describes how stream community structure changes:
options: Progressively from headwaters to the mouth, in response to changing physical conditions and energy sources
Randomly with no relationship to stream position
Only in response to fish migration
Identically at every point along the river
questions.correct_answer: Progressively from headwaters to the mouth, in response to changing physical conditions and energy sources
questions.explanation: The River Continuum Concept proposes a predictable longitudinal gradient in physical variables (width, depth, temperature, energy inputs) and associated biological communities from narrow, shaded headwater streams to wide, turbid lowland rivers.

questions.question: In a fast-flowing, shallow, turbulent, well-aerated stretch of a stream (as opposed to a deep, slow pool), the habitat is termed a:
questions.explanation: Riffles are shallow, turbulent, fast-flowing, well-oxygenated stream reaches that alternate with deeper, slower pools, together creating the characteristic pool-riffle sequence of many streams.

questions.question: Organisms specially adapted to withstand strong current in rivers, such as flattened bodies, suckers or hooks for attachment, are described as showing adaptations to:
questions.explanation: Many lotic (river/stream) organisms show morphological and behavioural adaptations -- flattened or streamlined bodies, suckers, hooks, or positive rheotaxis -- to resist being swept away by current and to exploit flowing-water habitats.

questions.question: Gross primary productivity in an aquatic ecosystem refers to:
options: The total rate of organic matter (carbon) fixation by photosynthesis, before subtracting respiratory losses
The rate of decomposition of dead organic matter
The rate of oxygen consumption by fish only
The total biomass of zooplankton present
questions.correct_answer: The total rate of organic matter (carbon) fixation by photosynthesis, before subtracting respiratory losses
questions.explanation: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total amount of organic matter produced by photosynthesis per unit time; net primary productivity (NPP) is GPP minus the producers' own respiratory losses.

questions.question: The classic light-and-dark bottle method for measuring aquatic primary productivity relies on measuring changes in:
options: Dissolved oxygen concentration in illuminated versus darkened water samples over time
questions.correct_answer: Dissolved oxygen concentration in illuminated versus darkened water samples over time
questions.explanation: In the light-and-dark bottle technique, oxygen produced by photosynthesis minus respiration is measured in a clear (light) bottle, while a black (dark) bottle records respiration alone; the difference allows estimation of gross and net productivity.

questions.question: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is used as a water quality indicator because it measures:
options: The amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter in a water sample over a set period
The total dissolved solids in water
The temperature fluctuation of a water body
questions.correct_answer: The amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter in a water sample over a set period
questions.explanation: BOD (commonly measured over 5 days, BOD5) estimates the oxygen-demanding organic pollution load of water; high BOD indicates heavy organic contamination (e.g. sewage) likely to deplete dissolved oxygen and stress aquatic life.

questions.question: Organisms such as certain mayfly and stonefly larvae, which are intolerant of pollution and low oxygen, are useful as:
options: Biological indicators of good water quality
Indicators of high water temperature only
questions.correct_answer: Biological indicators of good water quality
questions.explanation: Pollution-sensitive taxa (e.g. many mayflies, stoneflies, caddisflies) are used as bioindicators; their presence suggests clean, well-oxygenated water, while their absence and dominance by tolerant taxa (e.g. some midge larvae, worms) suggests organic pollution.

questions.question: Turbidity in a water body, measured in NTU (nephelometric turbidity units), primarily indicates:
options: The amount of suspended particulate matter reducing water clarity
The nitrogen content of the water
questions.correct_answer: The amount of suspended particulate matter reducing water clarity
questions.explanation: Turbidity measures the cloudiness of water caused by suspended particles (silt, algae, organic matter), which scatters light and can reduce the depth of the euphotic zone and smother benthic habitats.

questions.question: A Secchi disc is a simple limnological instrument used to measure:
questions.explanation: The Secchi disc, a black-and-white weighted disc lowered into the water, is used to estimate transparency from the depth at which it disappears from view, providing a simple proxy for turbidity and euphotic depth.

questions.question: A plankton net used for sampling zooplankton and phytoplankton typically has a mesh size designed to:
options: Retain organisms of a target size range while allowing water to pass through
questions.correct_answer: Retain organisms of a target size range while allowing water to pass through
questions.explanation: Plankton nets are made of fine mesh of a specified pore size that concentrates plankton of a chosen size class from a known volume of filtered water, enabling quantitative sampling.

questions.question: An Ekman grab (or Ekman dredge) is a sampling device used in limnology primarily to collect:
options: Benthic organisms and sediment from the lake or river bottom
questions.correct_answer: Benthic organisms and sediment from the lake or river bottom
questions.explanation: The Ekman grab is a spring-loaded sampler lowered to the substrate that closes to take a defined-area sample of bottom sediment together with the benthic organisms living in it.

questions.question: Wetlands such as floodplain swamps and marshes are ecologically important mainly because they:
options: Act as nutrient sinks/filters, flood buffers and highly productive habitats for diverse flora and fauna
Consist entirely of open deep water with no vegetation
questions.correct_answer: Act as nutrient sinks/filters, flood buffers and highly productive habitats for diverse flora and fauna
questions.explanation: Wetlands filter and retain nutrients and sediments, buffer flood peaks by storing excess water, and are among the most biologically productive ecosystems, supporting rich plant and animal diversity.

questions.question: The food web relationship in which phytoplankton are consumed by zooplankton, which are in turn consumed by planktivorous fish, illustrates:
options: A grazing food chain within the pelagic (limnetic) zone
questions.correct_answer: A grazing food chain within the pelagic (limnetic) zone
questions.explanation: This sequence (primary producer to primary consumer to secondary consumer) is a classic grazing food chain, distinct from detrital food chains that begin with dead organic matter decomposed by detritivores and decomposers.

questions.question: In many Nigerian reservoirs and lakes (e.g. Kainji Lake), the construction of a dam for hydroelectric power and irrigation exemplifies which type of lake formation?
questions.explanation: Reservoirs such as Kainji Lake are artificial lentic water bodies created by damming a river for purposes such as hydroelectric power, irrigation and fisheries, and they show ecological succession and limnological features distinct from natural lakes.
